title: No stranger anywhere
hookLine: no one is my enemy and no one a stranger; I get along with all (Kanara, ang 1299)

lines: THE FIRST DAY IN A NEW PLACE.
cards: The first day in a new place. A new school, a new job, a new country. Everyone else knows where the bathrooms are and who sits with whom.
You're the stranger. Now the other side: the day a stranger walks into your place, and you have to decide whether to smile.

For two weeks this path has followed Sikhs who were strangers almost everywhere they went: Hong Kong, Vancouver, Stockton, Southall. Today, a line from Guru Arjan turns the whole idea of stranger inside out.

teach.b: The hymn is by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, in Raag Kanara, on page one thousand two hundred ninety-nine of the Guru Granth Sahib.
It begins with a confession: I've forgotten all my envy of others, since I found the company of the holy. Then comes the line: Na ko bairi nahi bigana, sagal sang ham kau ban aai.
No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone. Bairi is an enemy.
Bigana is a stranger, an outsider, someone who isn't one of us. And the Guru says there aren't any.
Not because everyone is nice, but because of what comes next in the hymn: the one God is present in everyone, and seeing that, again and again, Nanak blossoms.

teach.h: THE ONE LIGHT IN EVERY FACE.
teach.b: If the same light is in every face, nobody is a stranger, just someone you haven't met.
Notice where this way of seeing comes from: the sangat. The Guru says it arrived with holy company. You don't get there alone, by thinking; you get there by sitting with people.
They came as strangers to Malaya and Canada and California and Britain. They were turned away from harbors, refused citizenship, told to take off their turbans, attacked.
And again and again they opened a room, installed the Guru, cooked langar, and fed whoever walked in, including the people who had treated them as strangers.
That closes this path's look at the diaspora, from leaving Punjab to kitchens at every border.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's hymn in Raag Kanara (Ang 1299) in kirtan, and many quote its line 'na ko bairi nahi bigana' as a summary of how the Gurus asked them to see others.

o: an enemy who means you real harm
a stranger, an outsider, not one of us
a pilgrim who travels to holy places

games.q: the line from ang 1299 — tap the pairs.
p: where this way of seeing came

s: the hymn says everyone is simply nice
it says God is present in everyone; that's why no one is a stranger.
the Guru says this way of seeing came through the sangat
since I found the company of the holy, the hymn begins.
the hymn is by Guru Nanak
it is by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, in Raag Kanara.

games.q: in the hymn, the Guru has lost all envy of others and sees no enemy or stranger. what does he say brought that change?
o: finding the company of the holy.
games.why: the hymn says it came since he found the sangat, the company of the holy: you learn it by sitting with people.

practice: Picture someone you'll probably see today but don't know: a cashier, a bus driver, a new face at work, someone on your street, and see their face as clearly as you can.
Now picture greeting them the way you'd greet a cousin you haven't seen in a while: a real smile, their name if you know it. Notice what shifts in you.

wordCard.voice: Bigana. A stranger or outsider — na ko bairi nahi bigana: no one is my enemy and no one a stranger; I get along with all.

carryVoice: Your line: no one is a stranger. That's day three hundred twenty-five.
